title: The Former Captive
author: William Saville
content:
Nadia raised a trembling hand to shield her sensitive blue eyes from the sunlight. It was blinding, a sharp contrast to the oppressive dimness she had endured for years. Natural light had become alien to her, a painful reminder of the freedom she had lost and the world she had almost forgotten.

Her captors had kept her in a concrete tomb, a place of constant dampness and decay. A single flickering bulb hung far across the cavernous room, its feeble light barely reaching the corner where her chains rattled against the wall. Her "bed" had been nothing more than a heap of moldy blankets, their putrid stench as unrelenting as the cold that seeped into her bones.

Her once-golden hair, now a filthy tangle of knots and grime, hung past the small of her back, marking the passage of time more clearly than the scars that laced her body or the sharp angles of her starved frame. She had been kept alive; barely. Meals of watery gruel had come sporadically, interspersed with brutal interrogations. They demanded secrets, and at first, she resisted, clinging to the loyalty ingrained in her as a government scientist.

But loyalty had its limits, and pain had none.

When her screams no longer echoed in the empty room, she began to speak. Classified information, details of top-secret projects she had spent her life developing, spilled from her cracked lips in exchange for morsels of food and moments of respite. Her government had presumed her dead, halting their search early, and that abandonment cut deeper than any torture.

Eventually, her secrets ran dry, but the war her captors waged against her homeland did not. With her knowledge, they gained the upper hand. Still, they saw value in her expertise; her unparalleled programming skills, her intricate knowledge of advanced weaponry. They didn’t kill her. Instead, they offered her a choice: stay in chains and die in filth or work for them.

For Nadia, it wasn’t a choice at all.

The sunlight remained harsh, even behind the tinted lenses of the sunglasses they had provided her. Nadia ran her hands over the coarse, unfamiliar fabric of the new clothes they’d given her, clean and functional but devoid of personality. Her captors; her new employers; had promised her freedom within strict limits: a monitored apartment, controlled transportation, regulated purchases, and no unapproved communications. It was freedom in name only, but after years of captivity, it felt like luxury.

A car with darkened windows waited at the curb. She hesitated before stepping inside, clutching the papers she had signed; papers that surrendered her independence in exchange for a fragile new life.

The appointments came in quick succession.

First, they shaved her matted hair, the weight of it falling from her scalp like a burden she had carried too long. She flinched at the sensation of clippers against her skin, but when they scrubbed her scalp clean, the unexpected gentleness of the act brought tears to her eyes. The buzzing dreadlocks were replaced with an expensive wig, its strands so close to her natural color that it felt like reclaiming a piece of herself.

Next came the tanning salon, where artificial light sought to restore the healthy glow her pallid skin had lost. Every step was calculated to make her look less like a survivor of torment and more like the poised, efficient scientist she once was.

A week later, Nadia sat behind a polished oak desk, staring at two sleek monitors. Her fingers flew over the keyboard as she wrote lines of complex code, her mind focused on the intricate programming needed to perfect the weaponry her new employers demanded.

She paused, her hand drifting to her stomach, where hunger gnawed at her; a reminder of a past she was still learning to leave behind. Crossing the room, she opened the mini fridge and pulled out a protein shake, its metallic taste a small price for nourishment. She drank it quickly, wiping her mouth with the back of her hand before returning to the task at hand.

Deadlines loomed. They always did.

As the days passed, Nadia began to settle into the routine, her body adjusting to the comforts she hadn’t dared to imagine during her captivity. But the weight of her choices lingered. Every keystroke on her keyboard was a betrayal of the country she had once served, the ideals she had once believed in. Yet, there was a dark exhilaration in the work; a thrill in problem-solving, in creating something powerful, even if it was for the wrong side.

Her polished exterior; manicured nails, sleek wig, tailored clothes; was a mask, hiding the fractured woman beneath. At night, in the quiet of her new apartment, she would lie awake, staring at the ceiling, haunted by the faces of her former colleagues, the memories of the tortures she had endured, and the knowledge of what her creations would unleash.

One morning, as she coded a particularly lethal sequence, she caught her reflection in the monitor’s black screen. The image stared back at her: clean, composed, and utterly unrecognizable.

For a moment, she hesitated, her hands hovering over the keys. Then, with a slow, deliberate movement, she began typing again.

There was no going back.
